title: Groundnut Stew, Adapted
author: Michael Twitty
desc: A declared adaptation with a full cup of peanut butter and both palm oil and a marinade — reduce the liquid by one third, stirring every fifteen minutes.
longDesc: This is a food historian's version and he says plainly it is his own way, written after eating the dish at a chop bar in Kumasi. The chicken is marinated with quartered red onion, smashed garlic, a ginger knob, a hot pepper, a stock cube, tomato paste and oil, then sautéed twenty minutes. Palm oil, broth, a full cup of unsweetened peanut butter, tomatoes, bay leaves and thyme go in, and the whole thing simmers forty-five minutes on low, stirred every fifteen minutes, until the liquid has reduced by one third. The cup of peanut butter makes this the thickest documented version.
ingredients: 2 lb boneless chicken breasts, or bone-in thighs and legs
1 stock cube, or 2 tsp powdered broth
2 large chopped tomatoes, or a 28 oz tin
steps: Combine the marinade ingredients with the chicken.
Add the palm oil, broth, peanut butter, tomatoes, bay leaves and thyme.
Simmer 45 minutes on low, stirring every 15 minutes.
The liquid should reduce by one third.
If using any optional umami additions, cook 10 minutes more.
chefTips: A full cup of peanut butter to two pounds of chicken is the richest documented ratio — roughly double the leanest. Expect a stew you can stand a spoon in, not a soup.
Reduced by one third is the cue, and it is the only documented groundnut soup that gives a volume endpoint rather than an oil-separation one.
Stir every fifteen minutes, which the author specifies. At this peanut concentration it will catch on the base otherwise.
Both palm oil and vegetable oil are used, in the stew and the marinade respectively. The palm oil is for colour and flavour rather than cooking.
Bay leaves and thyme are this author's additions and are not part of traditional nkatenkwan. Leave them out if you want the Ghanaian version.
It is a declared adaptation — 'My Way' is in the title — and the headnote credits a chop bar in Kumasi as the original. Treat it as a documented diaspora interpretation rather than a Ghanaian recipe.
His yield note is worth repeating as published: serves four to six, or two Ghanaians.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a traditional recipe rather than the declared adaptation it is.
Stopping before the liquid has reduced by a third.
sources: Adapted from 'Groundnut Stew My Way', byline as printed 'michaelwtwitty', afroculinaria.com, 26 March 2018. The author is the food historian Michael W. Twitty; the byline prints as his username. Yield as printed: 'Serves 4-6 (or 2 Ghanaians)'.

AUTHOR-DECLARED ADAPTATION, and published as one: 'My Way' is in the title. The headnote frames the dish as Akan, cites the spelling 'nkantenkwan', and credits a visit to 'Cece's chop bar in Kumasi'. It is a documented diaspora interpretation by a named food historian rather than a traditional Ghanaian recipe, and is filed as such.

Ingredients exactly as printed. Marinade: 2 pounds boneless chicken breasts or bone-in thighs/legs; 1 large red onion, quartered; 4 garlic cloves, smashed; 2-inch ginger knob; 1 small fresh hot pepper; 1 Maggi cube (or 2 teaspoons powdered broth); 1 teaspoon coarse black pepper; 2 tablespoons tomato paste; 2 tablespoons vegetable oil. Stew: 2 tablespoons palm oil; 2 cups vegetable or beef broth; 1 cup unsweetened peanut butter; 2 large chopped tomatoes (or 28-ounce can); 2-3 bay leaves; 2-3 thyme sprigs.

Method as printed: sauté the chicken 20 minutes; add the rest and simmer 45 minutes on low, stirring every 15 minutes. DONENESS CUE as printed: 'Liquid should reduce by one-third.' Optional umami additions get 10 further minutes.

THE ENDPOINT IS DIFFERENT IN KIND from the other documented groundnut soups, and that is recorded rather than harmonised: this recipe gives a VOLUME reduction (one third) where Adjonyoh, Atadika and the Mama Juliet version all give OIL SEPARATION. Neither is corrected toward the other.
NON-TRADITIONAL ADDITIONS, flagged: bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Neither appears in any other documented version of this dish.

PEANUT RATIO POSITION: 1 cup peanut butter to 2 lb chicken is the richest of the six documented versions, against ⅔ cup to a whole chicken at the leanest (GHA015). For the full spread see the sources at GHA013.
reheating: Low heat with broth or water to loosen. It thickens considerably when cold.
healthBenefits: Peanuts supply monounsaturated fat, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
Red palm oil contributes provitamin-A carotenoids.
Thyme and bay both carry antioxidant compounds, non-traditional though they are here.
culturalNote: A named food historian publishing his own version and labelling it as such is the honest way to adapt a dish, and it makes the recipe more useful rather than less — you can see exactly where he departed. The yield note, serves four to six or two Ghanaians, is also the best joke in the source material for this country.
